prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: EN · Long headers, short data (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 5 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 13px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Region" · longest unbreakable word 44px · one-line width 44px
  col 2: header "Quarterly revenue (USD, millions)" · longest unbreakable word 60px · one-line width 212px
  col 3: header "Year-over-year growth rate" · longest unbreakable word 45px · one-line width 172px
  col 4: header "Number of active enterprise customers" · longest unbreakable word 67px · one-line width 248px
  col 5: header "Net promoter score" · longest unbreakable word 59px · one-line width 124px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 619px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 618px.
Fixed: content, font, 13px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"excellent","why":"All headers fit in two lines, with balanced widths and compact rows that make comparisons easy."},"B":{"grade":"excellent","why":"The two-line headers and compact body produce a clear, balanced table; the slightly wider customer column suits its longer label."},"C":{"grade":"poor","why":"The customer header is squeezed into four lines while the revenue column has ample space, creating an uneven, overly tall header."},"D":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"The table scans clearly, but the customer and promoter headers each take three lines, making the header taller than necessary."},"E":{"grade":"poor","why":"The wide region column leaves little room for longer headers; revenue takes three lines and customers four, producing an uneven header."},"F":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Every header fits in two lines, and the widths give the longer customer label suitable room while keeping the data easy to scan."}},"best":["A","B","F"],"confidence":"high","unsure":"A, B and F differ only slightly in column proportions; the images do not establish a decisive preference among them."}
